concepts.title: Isolation of Nucleic Acids from Cells

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Isolation of Nucleic Acids from Cells' refers to.
questions.a: Extracting DNA or RNA means rupturing the boundary, shielding the treasure and purifying it: lysozyme digests bacterial walls, SDS or CTAB dissolves membranes while CTAB's ionic strength swaps DNA for polysaccharides, EDTA starves nucleases of divalent ions at mild alkaline pH, chloroform-isoamyl deproteinisation splits phases, and chilled ethanol drops the nucleic acid out of solution - with GITC-phenol-chloroform preferentially pulling RNA into the aqueous phase.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Isolation of Nucleic Acids from Cells'.
questions.a: Break the wall, block the nucleases, split the phases and precipitate - four moves that free intact nucleic acid from any cell.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Isolation of Nucleic Acids from Cells' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 3.2 (source: lebt103.txt section 3.2, Figs. 3.1-3.2, Box 1)

concepts.title: Restriction Enzymes Types and Cleavage Distances

questions.q: Using the method 'Restriction Enzymes Types and Cleavage Distances', work with: end_site = 10, start_site = 6, type1_distance = 12, type3_distance = 120. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of site_span.
questions.a: 4 years

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Restriction Enzymes Types and Cleavage Distances' and work with: end_site = 400, start_site = 4, type1_distance = 60, type3_distance = 100. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of site_span.
questions.a: 396 years

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Restriction Enzymes Types and Cleavage Distances' refers to.
questions.a: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific 4-8 bp recognition sites, mostly palindromic, and fall into three classes: Type I cleaves randomly around a thousand bases away with SAM, magnesium and ATP, Type II cuts precisely within the site needing only magnesium - hence its starring role in cloning - and Type III cuts some twenty-four to twenty-six bases away; names encode the source microbe, genus, species, strain and discovery order as in EcoRI or HindIII.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Restriction Enzymes Types and Cleavage Distances'.
questions.a: Only Type II cuts inside its recognition site; compare the cut distances of Types I and III to see how far off-target they work.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Restriction Enzymes Types and Cleavage Distances', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: distance_ratio = type1_distance / type3_distance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Enzyme Toolkit for DNA Manipulation' refers to.
questions.a: Beyond the cutters, cloning borrows a whole enzyme bench: DNA ligase seals 5-phosphate to 3-hydroxyl using ATP or NAD, DNA polymerase extends only from a primer's free 3-OH end, alkaline phosphatase strips terminal phosphates while polynucleotide kinase restores them, terminal transferase adds template-free homopolymer tails, reverse transcriptase copies RNA into cDNA, and poly-A polymerase adenylates RNA ends.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Enzyme Toolkit for DNA Manipulation'.
questions.a: Every joining, filling, tailing and copying job has a dedicated enzyme - match the chemistry to the tool.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Enzyme Toolkit for DNA Manipulation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 3.3 (source: lebt103.txt section 3.3 (iii)-(ix), Figs. 3.5-3.8)

concepts.title: Modes of DNA Transfer into Hosts

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Modes of DNA Transfer into Hosts' refers to.
questions.a: Nature moves DNA three ways - transformation by direct uptake, transduction by hitchhiking phage, and conjugation through an F-pilus bridging donor to recipient - and the laboratory extends the menu with calcium chloride heat shock, electric-pulse electroporation, liposome fusion, direct microinjection into the nucleus and gene-gun bombardment of DNA-coated gold particles.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Modes of DNA Transfer into Hosts'.
questions.a: Pick the delivery route by the host - chemical cocktails for bacteria, pores or bullets for stubborn walls and membranes.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Modes of DNA Transfer into Hosts' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 3.4 (source: lebt103.txt section 3.4, Figs. 3.9-3.12)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Screening Recombinants by Insertional Inactivation' refers to.
questions.a: Because only a lucky few cells receive the right construct, screening exploits lost functions: direct selection keeps antibiotic-resistant transformants alive, insertional inactivation knocks out a marker gene when the insert lands inside it - tetracycline plates keep all transformants while ampicillin replica plates expose those whose ampR was wrecked - and blue-white screening reads lacZ, where intact enzyme turns X-gal blue and disrupted lacZ leaves recombinant colonies white; GFP offers a fluorescent variant.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Screening Recombinants by Insertional Inactivation'.
questions.a: Whichever marker the insert breaks tells you which plate or colour hides the recombinant colony.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Screening Recombinants by Insertional Inactivation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 3.5 (source: lebt103.txt section 3.5, Figs. 3.13-3.14)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Blotting Techniques Southern Northern Western' refers to.
questions.a: Blotting pins molecules onto nitrocellulose, nylon or PVDF membranes for probing: Edwin Southern's capillary transfer finds DNA sequences with labelled probes; northern blotting of 1977 does the same for RNA on charged nylon with formamide buffer; and Burnette's 1981 western runs SDS-PAGE proteins onto membrane and flags the target with a specific antibody - together tracing a gene, its transcript and its protein, with the eastern blot spotting post-translational modifications.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Blotting Techniques Southern Northern Western'.
questions.a: Southern asks about DNA, northern about RNA, western about protein - same membrane logic, different probe.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Blotting Techniques Southern Northern Western' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 3.6 (source: lebt103.txt section 3.6, Figs. 3.15-3.17, Box 3)

questions.q: Using the method 'PCR Amplification Arithmetic', work with: cycles = 15, template_count = 6. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of net_new.
questions.a: 196602 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'PCR Amplification Arithmetic' and work with: cycles = 10, template_count = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of net_new.
questions.a: 306900 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'PCR Amplification Arithmetic' refers to.
questions.a: Kary Mullis's polymerase chain reaction photocopies DNA exponentially through thermal cycling - strands separate near 95 degrees Celsius, primers anneal around 50-55, and Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus extends at 72 - so the copy count doubles every cycle toward two raised to the cycle number, with real-time qPCR trading gels for SYBR-green fluorescence and Ct values that fall as template rises.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'PCR Amplification Arithmetic'.
questions.a: Multiply the starting molecules by two raised to the cycle number; a low Ct betrays abundant template.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'PCR Amplification Arithmetic', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: copies = template_count * 2 ** cycles

questions.q: Using the method 'Candidate Genes and DNA Libraries', work with: gene_bp = 75, genome_bp = 8, haploid_bp = 100. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of diploid_bp.
questions.a: 200 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Candidate Genes and DNA Libraries' and work with: gene_bp = 24, genome_bp = 80, haploid_bp = 360. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of diploid_bp.
questions.a: 720 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Candidate Genes and DNA Libraries' refers to.
questions.a: Finding one 3000-3500 bp gene inside a 3.2 billion base haploid genome is a needle-in-haystack problem, solved by hunting candidate genes tied to disease or agronomic traits and by banking clones: a genomic library houses every fragment of the genome, while a cDNA library made through reverse transcriptase stores only the intron-free transcripts active in a chosen tissue, ready as probes or expression templates.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Candidate Genes and DNA Libraries'.
questions.a: Divide genome size by gene size to measure the search problem, then let genomic or cDNA libraries shrink it to a shelf.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Candidate Genes and DNA Libraries', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: genome_fold = genome_bp / gene_bp
